questions.scenario: A Python app must call Azure AI Search without hard-coding its URL or credentials. The search service is connected to the Foundry project.
questions.question: How should the app obtain the search endpoint?

options.text: Ask the user to type the endpoint at start-up
options.why: This is not a reasonable design for an application.

options.text: Read the endpoint from the model deployment
options.why: Deployments do not hold search endpoints.

options.text: Call project.connections.get with the connection name
options.why: Correct. The connection stores the target and authentication method.

options.text: Copy the URL into a constant in the source file
options.why: This hard-codes the value and needs a change per environment.

questions.explanation: Connections keep targets and authentication details out of code.

questions.scenario: The same code must run on a developer laptop and in Azure without any key.
questions.question: Which credential should the code use?

options.why: The requirement is no key.
This is a storage mechanism and does not authenticate to Foundry.
Foundry requires authentication.
Correct. It uses the developer sign-in locally and a managed identity in Azure.

questions.explanation: DefaultAzureCredential tries several sources in order, which keeps code the same across environments.

questions.scenario: An agent app must export traces to Application Insights, and the instrumentation needs the connection string.
questions.question: Where can the app obtain it through the SDK?

options.why: Index schemas do not contain it.
Instructions are not configuration storage.

options.text: From the project telemetry methods, by using the Application Insights connection
options.why: Correct. The project knows which Application Insights resource is connected.
The deployment name does not hold a connection string.

questions.explanation: A connected Application Insights resource lets the SDK discover the trace destination.
